correctness.rationale: Direct differentiation with w=−z, r=y/x² and h=wx gives w'=4x, x'=−wrx², r'=1−r+2hr², h'=h²(4/w²−r). The respective signs at w=3, r=1/2, r=2 and h=1/10 are strictly inward (the upper r derivative is at most −1/5 and h'≤−h²/18). On every finite interval x≤x0 and w≤w0+4x0t, so (1/x)'=wr is bounded there and x cannot hit zero. All coordinates stay finite on bounded times, proving forward-global continuation, including boundary initial data. The h bound implies h→0; if w≤W, then x≥1/(1/x0+2Wt) and w'=4x contradicts bounded w. Variation of constants gives r→1 since 2hr²→0. Thus (1/h)'→1, implying th→1, and (w²)'=8h yields w²/(8 log t)→1 by integral comparison. The equivalents follow from x=h/w and y=rx². The allowed set contains an open subset, but includes boundary points. Frozen check.py was inspected, not executed: its line 13 is a no-op, so the claimed automatic check of the lower-r face should not be credited. The exact sign there is 1/2+h/2>0 by the proof, so the flaw does not affect the theorem.

value.rationale: The equilibrium-line degeneration raises the natural question whether projected convergence toward the line forces a finite equilibrium limit. The theorem constructs an open basin of forward-global exceptions and gives all three coordinate rates in physical time with universal leading constants. This is a quantitative dynamical distinction not fixed by the equilibrium classification or merely locating a point at infinity. It is not a global basin or sharp trapping-bound claim.
